case.case_title: Abasin Banda v. S. I. Gunaratne & Others

clause.text: No person shall be subjected to torture or to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the petitioner was subjected to torture or cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment in violation of Article 11 of the Constitution during his arrest and detention by the police.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner alleged that he was unlawfully arrested without reason, assaulted with a piece of wood and a broken chair leg by the 1st respondent, forced to consume alcohol, given urine to drink, and suffered injuries amounting to cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment in violation of Article 11.
case_context.respondent_argument: The 1st respondent denied arresting or assaulting the petitioner. The 2nd respondent claimed he arrested the petitioner for drunken and disorderly behavior and produced affidavits from witnesses supporting that the petitioner was intoxicated and abusive.
key_facts: Petitioner was arrested on 1 March 1995 at about 6 p.m. without being informed of the reason.
Petitioner was assaulted by the 1st respondent with a piece of wood and a broken chair leg causing injuries.
Petitioner was forced to swallow arrack and given urine to drink by the 1st respondent.
Petitioner was produced before the Magistrate the next morning, after an overnight detention.
Medical report confirmed non-grievous injuries caused by blunt weapons consistent with assault.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The court interpreted Article 11 as prohibiting torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment or punishment by public officials. The evidence showed the petitioner was subjected to such treatment by the 1st respondent while in custody, violating Article 11.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The court found the petitioner’s version credible and supported by medical evidence, rejecting the respondents’ denials and affidavits. The assault and degrading treatment inflicted by the 1st respondent constituted a violation of Article 11. The 2nd respondent, as officer-in-charge, was held responsible for acquiescing in the assault by failing to act.
principles_established: Article 11 protects individuals from torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment by state officials.
Police officers can be held personally liable for violations of Article 11.
Compensation serves to express societal abhorrence and provide some retribution for victims.
The State has obligations under the UN Convention on Torture to prevent such violations.
precedents_cited: Pelawattage (AAL) for Piyasena v. OIC Wadduwa

outcome.holding: The court declared that the petitioner’s fundamental right under Article 11 was violated by the 1st respondent. The 1st respondent and the State were ordered to pay compensation to the petitioner.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: The State was ordered to pay Rs. 20,000 and the 1st respondent Rs. 8,000; the 2nd respondent was also ordered to pay Rs. 8,000 for the assault. Additional sums were ordered for infringement of Articles 13(1) and 13(2) and costs, totaling Rs. 43,000.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 11 is central to the court’s reasoning as it directly prohibits the torture and cruel, inhuman or degrading treatment the petitioner suffered. The court’s finding of violation under Article 11 was dispositive of the claim for relief related to the assault and treatment in custody.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The petitioner was assaulted with a piece of wood and a broken chair leg by the 1st respondent, forced to swallow arrack, given urine to drink, and sustained injuries confirmed by medical report P1. The 2nd respondent was aware and acquiesced in the assault.
